title: Primary decomposition of a principal ideal in a Krull domain
statement: A commutative integral domain $A$ is called Krull if (i) for every height-one prime $P$ (a nonzero prime with no prime strictly between $(0)$ and $P$), $A_P$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime] is a Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring] normal domain [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring]; (ii) $A=\bigcap_{\mathrm{ht}(P)=1} A_P$ inside $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$; and (iii) every nonzero element of $A$ belongs to only finitely many height-one primes. An empty intersection inside a fraction field means that whole field. Let $D$ be a Krull domain and $0\ne b\in D$. The set of height-one prime ideals of $D$ containing $b$ is finite; write it as $P_1,\ldots,P_t$. Define $J_i=D\cap bD_{P_i}=\{x\in D:x/1\in bD_{P_i}\}$, the inverse image in $D$ of the principal ideal generated by $b/1$ in $D_{P_i}$. Then $bD=\bigcap_{i=1}^t J_i$ and $\sqrt{J_i}=P_i$ for each $i$, where $\sqrt J=\{x:x^n\in J\text{ for some }n\ge1\}$. When $t=0$, the ideal intersection means $D$.

Its minimal primary decomposition has components bD_P intersect D, whose radicals are the corresponding height-one primes P. Read online at https://www.math.purdue.edu/~iswanso/book/SwansonHuneke.pdf; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: By clause (iii) in the definition of a Krull domain, the nonzero element b belongs to only finitely many height-one primes. Enumerate precisely those primes as P_1, ..., P_t. If t=0, this list is empty and the later intersection convention is D.

Fix i. By the height-one localization dimension statement [lem-weil-pbc-localization-dimension-chains-below-prime], D_{P_i} is one-dimensional; clause (i) of the Krull definition makes it Noetherian and normal, and localization at P_i makes it local. Therefore [lem-sc-normal-dim1-dvr] makes D_{P_i} a discrete valuation ring. Since b∈P_i, b/1 is a nonunit. The existing DVR power statement [lem-weil-pbc-dvr-unit-times-uniformizer-power] gives bD_{P_i}=π_i^{n_i}D_{P_i} with n_i≥1, and its radical is the maximal ideal: writing m=(π_i), one has (π_i^{n_i})⊆m, so its radical is contained in the prime ideal m; conversely π_i^{n_i} belongs to (π_i^{n_i}), so π_i belongs to its radical and m is contained in that radical. The exponent is positive because exponent zero would make b/1 a unit. The localization-contraction statement [lem-trf-localization-maximal-contraction] identifies the contraction of that maximal ideal with P_i. Since J_i is the contraction of bD_{P_i}, contraction commutes with taking the radical here: x∈√J_i iff x/1∈√(bD_{P_i}). Hence √J_i=P_i.

proof.text: For x∈bD, write x=bd. Then x/1 belongs to bD_{P_i} for every i, so bD is contained in every J_i. Conversely, let x belong to every J_i. Then x/b lies in D_{P_i} for each height-one prime P_i containing b. If P is any other height-one prime, b∉P, so b is a unit in D_P and x/b∈D_P automatically. Thus x/b lies in every height-one localization of D. Clause (ii) of the Krull-domain definition gives x/b∈D, and therefore x∈bD. Hence bD=⋂_{i=1}^t J_i.

proof.text: When t=0, every height-one localization makes b a unit, so the same intersection argument gives bD=D; this is exactly the stipulated empty-intersection convention. The radicals statement is asserted only for the listed primes, so all clauses hold in the unit case as well.
